newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY MAY STEP UP ANTI-INFLATION FIGHT - MEDGYESSY.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY MAY STEP UP ANTI-INFLATION FIGHT - MEDGYESSY.

text.p: Hungary's government is likely to discuss within three weeks two alternative programmes about the reduction of inflation (CPI) in 1998, Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy told Reuters in an interview on Monday.
"This is a matter of such importance that before (the government discussion) I will ask the Prime Minister and the central bank president for a joint consultation," he said.

Medgyessy declined to disclose the details of the plans, but said that the alternative programme, which includes a more radical cut, may push down year-on-year inflation to slightly below 10 percent by December 1998 in the optimal case.

He said that a larger cut in inflation would be more favourable for economic growth adding that the other programme for 1998 would represent a one to three percentage point smaller cut in average inflation.

"The chance of that (larger inflation reduction) depends very much on what the social partners (employers and trade unions) are ready to accept and what parts of the anti-inflationary programme politicians are willing to undertake," he said.

He said that year-on-year inflation could go down to between 16 to 17 percent by December 1997 from 18.8 percent in March, adding that he would be able to give a more precise forecast in June, after seeing the May CPI figures.
Medgyessy said the ministry maintained its 18 percent average inflation forecast for 1997, compared with an average inflation of 23.6 percent last year.
The government, approving the draft of the pension reform last week, showed that it did not hesitate to make decisions for the long-term, although 1998 elections were near, he said.
"I think the government will be able to undertake the programme (including the larger inflation cut) despite the difficult situation," he said.
"I would rather ask whether the necessary confidence of the social partners can be created," he said. "I think that if they see guarantees (for the completion of the programme) they will agree."

Whichever of the two programmes is approved, government intervention would use only tools which are usual in market economies, such as decisions on interest rates and devaluation, the central bank's reserve policies and its open market interventions, Medgyessy said.
He said that declining inflation and structural reforms together would support increasing and sustainable economic growth.

Hungary targets a gross domestic product (GDP) growth of two to three percent this year, up from a prelimiary figure of one percent in 1996, and plans to boost growth to up to five percent in the next few years.
Hungary's deep structural reforms should help it avoid trade and current account problems which could arise from rising economic growth, Medgyessy said.
He said Hungary's economic restrictions introduced two years ago were necessary to create conditions for sustainable growth, but alone were not sufficient to spark growth.
He added that the government's decision about pensions also outlined measures in the health care system, but the health care reform itself was likely to come only after the 1998 elections.
The pension and health care reforms will be operational in 1998 and 1999 and guarantee that ecconomic growth is sustainable, Medgyessy said.
